title: 2025 Supervisory Stress Test Methodology
summary: The Federal Reserve publishes its 2025 Supervisory Stress Test Methodology document, detailing the models used to assess how large banks ($100B+ in assets) would perform under hypothetical severe recession scenarios. This document is part of the annual Dodd-Frank Act stress testing cycle and covers methodologies for projecting bank losses, revenues, and regulatory capital ratios. Results from applying these models are published separately in Q2.
key_points: Federal Reserve annually conducts supervisory stress tests as required by the Dodd-Frank Act
Applies to bank holding companies (BHCs), covered savings and loan holding companies (SLHCs), and intermediate holding companies (IHCs) with $100 billion or more in assets
Stress test cycle publishes four documents: Scenarios (mid-Feb), Methodology (June), Results (end Q2), and Capital Requirements (Q3)
Methodology covers models for projecting pre-tax net income, loan losses, and calculating regulatory capital ratios
Specific models described include: Corporate Loan Model, Commercial Real Estate Loan Model, Domestic First-Lien Residential Mortgage Model, and Domestic Credit Card Model
The stress test evaluates bank financial resilience by estimating losses, revenues, expenses, and resulting capital levels under hypothetical economic conditions
why_it_matters: This methodology document is foundational for understanding how the Federal Reserve assesses bank capitalization under stress. While it does not contain immediate market-moving information, it informs the capital requirements that ultimately affect how much banks can lend and their risk-taking capacity. Market participants monitoring bank sector resilience or anticipating capital requirement changes reference this document to understand the modeling assumptions underlying future results.
market_structure_context: The document describes supervisory frameworks for bank capital adequacy assessment, which shapes the structural resilience requirements for the largest U.S. financial institutions. While not addressing market microstructure or trading venue operations, it defines the stress testing component of bank prudential regulation that influences market participants' assessment of systemic risk.
